🙈 Covering Oneself in the River — modesty versus denying Avraham's covenant
🚿 Rav Yehuda's Bathhouse Routine — natron, steam, and drinking the water
🫖 Mulyar vs. Antikhi — two heating vessels, two different Shabbat rulings

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Modesty, Health, and Two More Heating Vessels
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 41a–41b
overview.hebrewSource: מוּלְיָאר הַגָּרוּף שׁוֹתִין הֵימֶנּוּ בְּשַׁבָּת. אַנְטִיכֵי, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁגְּרוּפָה אֵין שׁוֹתִין הֵימֶנָּה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf closes out the discussion of bathing with stories about Rabbi Abbahu's modest conduct in the river and Rabbi Zeira's chance encounter with his teacher, Rav Yehuda, in the bathhouse. Two new mishnayot then introduce further heating vessels and their Shabbat rules: the mulyar and antikhi urns used for hot water, and the case of an emptied urn into which cold water may or may not be poured, depending on whether the goal is a gentle warming or something closer to actually heating — or even inadvertently 'tempering' — the metal itself.

slides.title: 🙈 May One Cover Oneself for Modesty in the River?
slides.subtitle: Descending versus emerging makes all the difference

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: Rav taught: anyone who places his hands over his genitals is as if he denies the covenant of Avraham — it looks like he's hiding his circumcision!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: No contradiction: while descending into the river, facing no one, covering oneself looks like denial — forbidden. While emerging, facing people on the bank, covering for modesty is permitted.

lines.speaker: In practice
lines.text: Rava would bend over when emerging; Rabbi Zeira stood upright even then.

lines.speaker: Rav Ashi's academy
lines.text: Stood upright while descending, and bent over only while emerging — matching the rule precisely.

callout.label: Why floating was allowed at all:
callout.text: Rabbi Abbahu's pool had embankments, making it look like an enclosed vessel rather than an open river — a baraita otherwise forbids floating even in a courtyard pool that lacks such borders.

slides.title: 🚿 Overhearing Rav Yehuda in the Bathhouse
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Zeira's search for one last teaching before leaving for Eretz Yisrael
slides.hebrewSource: פִּתְחוּ פּוּמַּיְיכוּ וְאַפִּיקוּ הַבְלָא, וְאִשְׁתוּ מִמַּיָּא דְּבֵי בָאנֵי
slides.label: What he heard:
slides.text: Rabbi Zeira, planning to move to Eretz Yisrael against his teacher's view that doing so violated a positive commandment (Jeremiah 27:22), wanted to hear something from Rav Yehuda first without confronting him directly. He found him in the bathhouse instructing his attendants: 'Bring me natron, bring me a comb, open your mouths and let the steam out, and drink from the bathhouse water.' Rabbi Zeira said this alone was worth the visit. The Gemara explains each instruction: mundane requests may be spoken in the sacred tongue even in a bathhouse; releasing steam speeds sweating (הַבְלָא מַפֵּיק הַבְלָא); and drinking while bathing prevents the digestive harm of eating without drinking, walking, or later rinsing in cold water and oiling the skin.

slides.title: 🫖 Two Heating Vessels: Mulyar and Antikhi
slides.subtitle: New mishna — same swept status, opposite rulings
headers: May one drink from it, once swept of coals?
rows: Water on the inside, coals on the outside
A stove-like recess (bei chirei) built into a wall
Two stacked cauldrons: coals below, water above (bei dudei)
No — forbidden, because the copper itself continues to heat the water

callout.label: Why the difference matters:
callout.text: A baraita supports Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's identification, teaching explicitly that an antikhi is forbidden even swept and covered with ash, since its copper walls retain and conduct heat directly to the water.

slides.title: 🔥 The Emptied Urn: How Much Water May Be Added?
slides.subtitle: The mishna's apparent self-contradiction, resolved by quantity

nodes.content: ❓ Mishna: one may not add cold water to an emptied hot urn to heat it — yet one may add water to warm it. Which is it?
💡 Rav Adda bar Mattana resolves: it depends on the amount of water added

columns.label: Small quantity
columns.content: Forbidden — a small amount of cold water in a still-hot urn would itself become fully hot

columns.label: Large quantity
columns.content: Permitted — a large amount only loses its chill (l'hafshir), without truly heating up

slides.title: ⚒️ Does Adding Water 'Temper' the Urn Like Metalwork?
slides.subtitle: Abaye reframes the mishna, and Rav and Shmuel debate the resulting question

lines.speaker: Challenge
lines.text: Doesn't pouring cold water into a hot metal urn count as 'tempering' it — a form of the prohibited labor of finishing metal?

lines.speaker: First answer
lines.text: The mishna follows Rabbi Shimon: an unintended outcome (tempering) is permitted when one's actual intent was only to warm the water.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: That can't be right — the mishna's wording is 'an urn that was removed' (still holding hot water), not 'an urn emptied of water.' Properly read: adding water to an emptied urn is forbidden outright, and this follows Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids even unintended outcomes.

lines.speaker: Rav vs. Shmuel
lines.text: Rav: the leniency applies only up to the measure needed to warm the water, not to fill it enough to temper the metal. Shmuel: even filling to the tempering measure is permitted.

summary.principle: From modest conduct while bathing to the precise mechanics of heating vessels, the Gemara consistently asks not just what was done but what was intended — distinguishing denial of the covenant from modesty, drinking from cooking, and warming water from unintentionally tempering metal.

flowSteps.content: 🙈 Covering oneself is forbidden while descending into the river, permitted while emerging, for modesty
🚿 Rav Yehuda's bathhouse routine teaches both etiquette and health practice
🫖 A mulyar may be drunk from once swept; an antikhi may not, since its copper keeps heating the water

columns.content: 🔥 An emptied urn: small additions of water forbidden, large additions permitted
⚒️ Whether tempering the urn is itself forbidden splits Rav from Shmuel

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: intent and quantity, not just the physical act, determine whether an action counts as forbidden 'cooking' or 'tempering' on Shabbat

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, when is it permitted to cover one's genitals with one's hands while bathing in a river?
o: Never, under any circumstances
Only while descending into the water
Only while emerging from the water, facing people on the bank
Only if one is a priest
quiz.e: While descending (facing no one), covering oneself looks like denying Avraham's covenant and is forbidden; while emerging and facing onlookers, it is permitted for modesty.

quiz.q: Why was Rabbi Abbahu permitted to float in a particular pool despite the general prohibition on floating in water on Shabbat?
o: He was a Torah scholar and exempt from the rule
The pool had embankments, making it resemble an enclosed vessel rather than an open body of water
It was not actually Shabbat
Floating was always permitted for everyone
quiz.e: A baraita forbids floating in an open pool lacking embankments; Rabbi Abbahu's pool had them, distinguishing it from a river or ocean.

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what is the key difference between a mulyar and an antikhi once both are swept of coals?
o: There is no difference; both are permitted
One may drink from a swept mulyar, but not from a swept antikhi, since its copper continues to heat the water
The mulyar is always forbidden and the antikhi always permitted
Both are forbidden under all circumstances
quiz.e: A swept mulyar (water inside, coals outside) is permitted, while an antikhi remains forbidden because its copper construction keeps conducting heat to the water.

quiz.q: Regarding an urn emptied of its hot water, what does Rav Adda bar Mattana say determines whether adding cold water is permitted?
o: The time of day
The quantity of water added — a small amount becomes hot, a large amount only loses its chill
Whether the water is drawn from a well or a river
Whether a priest performs the action
quiz.e: A small quantity added would heat up fully in the still-hot urn (forbidden); a large quantity merely loses its chill without truly heating (permitted).

quiz.q: What is the dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding adding water to an emptied urn to the point of 'tempering' the metal?
o: Both permit it without any limit
Rav permits only up to the measure needed to warm the water; Shmuel permits even filling to the tempering measure
Both forbid it entirely
The dispute concerns only wooden vessels
quiz.e: Rav restricts the leniency to the amount needed merely to warm the water, while Shmuel permits even a quantity sufficient to temper (harden) the urn.
